tier_reason: The README Benchmark section runs pybase64 and the stdlib base64 module in the same process via the public CLI (src/pybase64/__main__.py, 'pybase64 benchmark'). It states the compiler (Apple clang 21.0.0, clang-2100.1.1.101), Python 3.15.0rc1 and the CPU (Apple M1 Max). Flags come from setup.py, which builds the bundled aklomp/base64 SIMD codec with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and the extension with Python's sysconfig CFLAGS, so A holds under the build-config-counts-as-flags precedent.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Default settings (altchars=None, validate=True, padded=True): b64encode 17,492 MB/s vs stdlib base64.b64encode 2,653 MB/s (~6.6x); b64decode with validate=True 9,037 MB/s vs 2,656 MB/s (~3.4x); encodebytes 6,595 vs 2,386 MB/s (~2.8x). With validate=False (the b64decode default in both libraries), decode is only 2,369 vs 2,030 MB/s (~1.17x). With padded=False or ignorechars=b'', decode is slower than stdlib, e.g. 2,521 vs 2,655 MB/s. Ratios derived from page data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101); Python 3.15.0rc1. Per setup.py, the bundled aklomp/base64 is built via CMake with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and the C extension with Python sysconfig CFLAGS. Exact flags are not printed in the README.
corrections.caveats: Compared against Python's own stdlib base64 module (a C-implemented binascii wrapper), not a C/C++ baseline. The speed comes from the bundled aklomp/base64 SIMD codec (a git submodule; aklomp/base64 is catalogued separately). The large decode win (~3.4x) needs validate=True. With default validate=False decode is ~1.17x, and several unpadded or ignorechars decode configurations are slower than CPython 3.15's stdlib. Encode (~6.6x) is the robust win. Numbers come from a single machine (Apple M1 Max, NEON path).

notes: The record's benchmark_url returned 404 because the repo's default branch is master, not main; I corrected it to the master README. All quoted numbers match the README exactly. Metadata checks out: BSD-2-Clause, 182 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, not archived and not a fork.

tier_reason: arXiv 2412.16398 is a single-author v1 preprint (cs.DS) and Crossref shows no peer-reviewed venue, so it is first-party evidence, not B. The repo has public benchmark code (test_crc.c, run_tests.sh; configure sets gcc CFLAGS=-O3) and the paper names the CPUs, but no gcc version is stated anywhere, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: CRC32 throughput increased by 100% (2x) across platforms vs the current state of the art (zlib 1.3.1.1 braiding) for table-less, non-hardware-accelerated CRC. Applying Chorba to hardware-accelerated (PCLMUL/AVX1 folding) implementations gives 5-20% depending on message length. The 2x applies to large messages; below a few MB the Chorba variants fall back to chorba_small and gains shrink. Per-size results appear only in figures.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. Repo configure/Makefile.in: gcc (version not stated) with CFLAGS=-O3, plus -mno-avx on x86_64 and -DAVX1_PCLMUL=1 / -DAVX2_PCLMUL=1 when the CPU supports them.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 5600 (desktop); AWS EC2 t4g.micro (Graviton2/Neoverse-N1); Raspberry Pi 4. AVX figures also on AMD Ryzen and Intel Skylake, with AVX512 discussed on an Intel Icelake server.
corrections.caveats: arXiv v1 preprint (cs.DS), no peer-reviewed venue found via Crossref. The compiler version is not stated; the repo builds with gcc -O3. Numeric results are only in figures, in seconds per 10^12 bytes, plus the abstract's summary. The 5-20% gain is for the PCLMUL/AVX1 path, not native CRC32-opcode platforms, which serve only as comparison points. The 2x holds for large messages, and destructive variants regress on the Raspberry Pi 4. zlib-ng 2.3.0 adopted Chorba (generic/SSE2/SSE4.1; PR #1837 by the author), but its release notes give no numbers.

notes: The paper's table confirms the zlib 1.3.1.1 braiding baseline, and the abstract's 100% and 5-20% figures match. The record overstated the 5-20% as covering native-CRC32-instruction platforms. The LICENSE file is the zlib license (GitHub reports NOASSERTION), so Zlib/copyable is right. 6 stars and the last commit of 2024-12-27 (stale) are confirmed.

tier_reason: Upgraded from B to A. The base64-benchmark harness is public (src/, CMakeLists.txt with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release and -mavx2 on the AVX2 file; build/msvc/base64.vcxproj Release|x64 with /O2 MaxSpeed and /arch:AVX2). The results page names the compiler and CPU for every run: MSVC 19.51 on an Intel Core i9-13900K @ 3.0 GHz, Clang 20.1.2 on Ubuntu 24.04 with an AMD Ryzen 7 5700G, and AppleClang 21 on a MacBook Air M4. It is not an independent suite, since the benchmark and library share an author, but A does not depend on who ran it.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Windows 32 KiB combined encode+decode: 11.155 GB/s vs aklomp/base64 9.118 GB/s (~1.22x), Turbo-Base64 10.206 GB/s (~1.09x) and simdutf 9.2.0 9.077 GB/s (~1.23x) (ratios derived from page data). Also leads Linux 32 KiB (9.802 GB/s) and ranks #2 on macOS (7.179 GB/s), each on different hardware.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Windows: MSVC 19.51 (VS 2026, v145 toolset), Release|x64, /O2 (MaxSpeed) with intrinsics and /arch:AVX2 on base64_avx2.c. Linux: Clang 20.1.2, CMake Release (-mavx2 on the AVX2 file). macOS: AppleClang 21, CMake Release.
corrections.hardware: Windows: Intel Core i9-13900K @ 3.0 GHz. Linux: Ubuntu 24.04, AMD Ryzen 7 5700G. macOS: MacBook Air M4 (named on gaspardpetit.github.io/base64-benchmark).
corrections.caveats: The benchmark repo and the winning library share an author (gaspardpetit), a conflict-of-interest risk. The library repo was created 2026-09-14 and has 0 stars. Cross-platform figures come from different machines and are not comparable. Margins over Turbo-Base64 (~9%) and aklomp/simdutf (~22%) are modest at a single 32 KiB point, and the author notes rankings change with compiler, size and operation. Malformed-input handling is not normalized across implementations.

notes: All quoted README numbers belong to the GaspardPetit SIMD row. The record wrongly said runs were on GitHub-hosted runners with no CPU model, but the published results page names the i9-13900K, Ryzen 7 5700G and M4 machines, which supports the upgrade to A.
